passage: I'm Rashmi, and I live in the flat next door, so our balconies almost touch. Baljeet came into that house as a bride three weeks ago. I keep seeing the same picture: Baljeet washing steel glasses that are already clean, then asking the mother-in-law, “Is this how you like it?” The father-in-law reads his paper and says nothing. The mother-in-law answers, “Fine, fine,” without looking up, which leaves Baljeet asking again. Yesterday the husband, Sanjay, took the glasses gently. “I'll dry tonight, Ma,” he said, and stood beside Baljeet at the sink. I can't say what Baljeet feels. But the shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What was Baljeet washing when Rashmi kept seeing the same picture?
qa.a: Baljeet was washing steel glasses that were already clean.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling when asking, “Is this how you like it?” again and again?
qa.a: Baljeet seems anxious about being judged in the new house and is asking for approval, though Rashmi says the inner feeling can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Sanjay do that helped, and why might it matter?
qa.a: Sanjay took the glasses, offered to dry and stood beside Baljeet at the sink. A spouse who stands beside a newcomer shows the house that the two are together.

qa.q: What might it be like for Baljeet when the mother-in-law says “Fine, fine” without looking up?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel unsure whether the answer is approval or not, which fits asking the same question again.

grounding: An observer describes a newly married person joining a household with unspoken habits, feeling watched, and helped when the spouse stands beside them.

passage:
Day 2. In his wife's family home, Pranav was told which chair was his and that he must wait for the elders to eat first. He nodded and stayed silent. Her aunts asked about his salary, his mother's cooking and his plans for children. Pema kept passing him water.
Day 9. Her uncle corrected how he folded the newspaper. Pranav smiled tightly and refolded it. That evening Pema said to her father, “Papa, he's a guest and a family member both. Let him choose his chair.” Her father grunted, then laughed.
Day 30. Pranav's chair was the one by the window, and he had started asking the aunts for recipes.

qa.q: Which chair did Pranav's hosts tell him was his on Day 2?
qa.a: On Day 2 he was told which chair was his and that he must wait for the elders to eat first.

qa.q: Why did Pranav smile tightly and refold the newspaper on Day 9?
qa.a: Pranav seems to feel watched and evaluated in the new house, so he goes along quietly instead of objecting.

qa.q: What did Pema do that helped Pranav settle in?
qa.a: Pema kept passing him water, then spoke up to her father so that Pranav could choose his chair, standing beside him.

qa.q: How might Pema's father have seen the change by Day 30?
qa.a: Her father may have come to see Pranav as part of the family, since he laughed after the chair remark and by Day 30 Pranav sat by the window and asked the aunts for recipes.

grounding: A newly married man joins his wife's household, feels watched and evaluated on Days 2 and 9, and settles in by Day 30 with his wife beside him.

passage:
Session note, community centre. Present: Jomon, his wife Anila, and Jomon's mother. The disagreement was about whether the couple should move into the family home. For the first twenty minutes Jomon looked at the floor and said, “Whatever you both think.” His mother and Anila each turned to him, then away, more upset each time he stayed silent. When I asked him to say what he wanted, he took a long breath. “Amma, I hear you. Anila and I will decide about the flat together, and you are welcome every Sunday.” Both women went quiet, then Amma nodded. I suggested the couple talk privately this week before returning.
Nandini, counsellor

qa.q: Who was present at the session besides Jomon?
qa.a: His wife Anila and Jomon's mother were present.

qa.q: Why did Jomon say, “Whatever you both think,” for the first twenty minutes?
qa.a: Jomon seems to be torn and trying to avoid the tension. Staying silent left his mother and Anila each feeling unsupported.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Anila do during the week before returning?
qa.a: They could talk privately about what they want and agree on a shared plan, so Jomon can speak fairly to his mother with Anila's view already heard.

qa.q: How might Jomon's mother have felt when Jomon said, “you are welcome every Sunday”?
qa.a: Jomon's mother may have felt reassured that she is not being pushed away, which fits her going quiet and then nodding.

grounding: A young spouse caught between his mother and his wife avoids the tension by silence, which leaves both unsupported, then takes a calm, fair stand.

passage:
Shalini's diary, Thursday, 11 pm.
Tonight my parents came to dinner and Papa said we should move within a short drive of them. Vishal said he'd like to keep our flat near his office. Then both of them looked at me. I kept passing chapatis. Papa said, “Beta, you decide.” Vishal said nothing and went out to the balcony. I stayed at the table with Mummy and heard myself say, “Let me think.” Now I see my silence helped nobody: it sounded like agreeing with nobody. Tomorrow I'll say to Papa, calmly, that we love them, that we are staying near Vishal's office, and that Sundays are theirs. Then I'll go and sit next to Vishal.

qa.q: Where did Vishal go after saying nothing?
qa.a: Vishal went out to the balcony.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when both Papa and Vishal looked at Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini felt torn and cornered by two views and passed chapatis instead of answering, and now sees that the silence helped nobody.

qa.q: What did the writer plan to do about it?
qa.a: Shalini plans to tell Papa calmly that they are staying near Vishal's office and that Sundays are for Papa and Mummy, then to sit beside Vishal.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Shalini said, “Let me think”?
qa.a: Vishal may have felt unsupported and left alone with the disagreement, which fits leaving for the balcony without a word.

grounding: A young spouse torn between their own parents and partner stays silent, sees that it left both unsupported, and plans a calm, fair stand.

passage:
Class note, couples' evening at the community hall. After last week's role-play, Vandana and her husband came back and told the group how it went when his parents visited. Before the visit they had agreed on two things: their salaries and the flat's plans stay between the two of them, and Sunday lunch is always open to the family. When the father-in-law asked about money, Vandana smiled and said, “That's ours to keep, Papa-ji, but we would love your advice on the kitchen.” Nobody raised a voice. Papa-ji laughed and asked for tea instead. The mother-in-law, at first stiff, was showing the couple her recipe book by evening. I asked the group what they had noticed.
Alka, class tutor

qa.q: What two things did Vandana and her husband agree on before the visit?
qa.a: They agreed that their salaries and the flat's plans stay between the two of them, and that Sunday lunch is open to the family.

qa.q: Why did Vandana add, “we would love your advice on the kitchen”?
qa.a: Vandana seems to want the refusal to feel warm and not like a wall, so she offers something the father-in-law can share in.

qa.q: What did the couple do that helped the boundary be accepted?
qa.a: They decided together beforehand, communicated kindly and gave the family a clear way to belong, so nobody felt shut out.

qa.q: How might the mother-in-law have felt by evening?
qa.a: The mother-in-law seems to have relaxed and felt included, since she was stiff at first and then showed the couple her recipe book.

grounding: A young couple agrees on what to share and what to keep private, then says so kindly to the in-laws, and the boundary is accepted.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Gurpreet's diary, Saturday night.
My husband Jomon and I sat on the balcony before his parents arrived and settled it: we will tell them about the housewarming, but not about how much rent we pay or what we saved. I practised the sentence three times. When his mother asked at lunch how much the flat costs, my hands went cold. I said, “Mummy-ji, that part we're keeping between us, but you are the first two we are inviting.” The room went still. His father put down the spoon. Then his mother said, “Achha, so which day?” and passed me the pickle. My heart is still pounding. Jomon squeezed my hand under the table. I think it went well.

qa.q: How many times did Gurpreet practise the sentence?
qa.a: Gurpreet practised the sentence three times.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when the flat's cost was asked about at lunch?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt nervous, with cold hands, and still spoke warmly. The pounding heart afterwards shows the strain. 😰

qa.q: What made the boundary easier to accept at that lunch?
qa.a: The couple had agreed together beforehand what to share and what to keep private, and Gurpreet added a warm invitation so the refusal did not feel like rejection.

qa.q: How might Jomon's mother have taken the words, “that part we're keeping between us”?
qa.a: She seems to have accepted it, since after the room went still she asked, “Achha, so which day?” and passed the pickle.

grounding: A young couple decides together what they will share and keep private and tells the in-laws kindly, and the boundary is accepted.

passage: Elizabeth found out on a bus ride back from the town market. Her brother Yash, who everyone thought was still working at the tile shop, had lost the job in spring and taken a loan from a local lender to keep up the pretence. Now the lender's man had begun calling at the house. Their parents thought the calls were for the shop. That evening, at the tea stall near the bus stand, she told only Aunt Mala, the retired schoolteacher, who listened without gasping. Later Elizabeth sat down with Yash. “I won't say it behind your back,” she said. “But they need to hear it before the man comes again. You tell them, and I sit beside you.”

qa.q: What had Yash lost in spring?
qa.a: Yash had lost the job at the tile shop in spring.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth worry about and want when deciding who should know?
qa.a: Elizabeth was weighing Yash's privacy against the parents' right to know before the lender's man came again. She also did not want to use the secret against him.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make about telling the parents?
qa.a: She asked Yash to tell them himself and offered to sit beside him, instead of speaking behind his back.

qa.q: How might Yash feel when Elizabeth says, “I sit beside you”?
qa.a: Yash may feel relieved that he is not left alone with it, though probably still ashamed, since he had kept up the pretence for months.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy against safety, asks a trusted person for support and does not use the secret as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Selin had read the letter twice before she folded it back into her late grandmother's box. It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born. Nobody had ever spoken of it. That night in the flat above the bakery, Selin's father was watching a match, and her mother was on the phone with a cousin. Selin did not say a word. On Sunday she met Abebe, an old family friend who had known her mother since school, at the park. “If she wants a sibling to know, that is hers to decide,” Abebe said. “Ask her gently, alone, and don't carry it as a weapon.” Selin nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did the letter in Selin's grandmother's box say?
qa.a: It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born.

qa.q: Why did Selin say nothing that night in the flat?
qa.a: Selin seems to want to protect her mother's privacy and think first before speaking, so she keeps the letter to herself for now.

qa.q: What could Selin do next after the talk with Abebe?
qa.a: Selin could ask her mother gently, when they are alone, and let her mother decide who else should know.

qa.q: How might Selin's mother feel if she found out that Selin knew?
qa.a: Selin's mother might feel exposed and worried at first, so speaking gently and privately, not in front of the family, would matter to her.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy and fairness, seeks a trusted person's advice and decides not to use the secret as a weapon.

passage: Ms Nair's class was doing fractions on the board. Pooja wasn't sure of the answer, but her hand went up anyway. “Three-sixths?” she said. “Not quite,” said the teacher, smiling, “but let's see how you got there.” Pooja explained, and the teacher wrote her steps on the board. “Look, Pooja found half the puzzle. Who can find the rest?” A boy giggled at the back. “We all learn by being wrong,” the teacher said mildly, and the giggle stopped. Abhinav, who never spoke in class, kept his hand low, though his eyes followed the chalk. Three more hands went up.

qa.q: What fraction did Pooja offer as her answer?
qa.a: Pooja offered “Three-sixths?” as her answer.

qa.q: Why did Pooja raise her hand even though she was not sure of the answer?
qa.a: Pooja seems to feel safe being wrong in this room, because mistakes here are treated as part of learning. 🙂

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped children keep volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher asked how Pooja got there, wrote her steps on the board, and stopped the giggle mildly while calling wrong answers a way to learn.

qa.q: What might Abhinav be thinking as his eyes follow the chalk while his hand stays low?
qa.a: Abhinav may be interested and slowly gaining trust that a wrong answer will be safe, but is not ready yet to speak.

grounding: A child in a warm classroom raises a hand though unsure because mistakes are treated as part of learning.

passage: I'm Harsha, and I sit two rows behind Harish. Harish hadn't put a hand up all term. Today the teacher asked what one-half plus one-quarter was, and Harish's hand went up slowly. “Two-sixths?” he said. I held my breath. Nobody laughed. The teacher wrote it on the board and said, “That's a very useful mistake. It shows us what happens when we add the bottoms.” Harish's ears turned red. I can't tell what he felt. But when the next question came, his hand went up again, a bit faster.

qa.q: Where does Harsha sit compared with Harish?
qa.a: Harsha sits two rows behind Harish.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when Harish's ears turned red?
qa.a: Harish may have felt exposed and shy after speaking, though Harsha can't be sure. The hand going up faster for the next question suggests the moment felt safe enough.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to keep Harish volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher could keep treating mistakes as useful, call on Harish when a hand goes up and praise the effort, not just the right answer.

qa.q: How might the class's silence have felt to Harish after the answer?
qa.a: It probably felt like relief: nobody laughed, so being wrong did not cost anything, which fits the quicker hand on the next question.

grounding: An observer watches a child who never volunteered answer unsure in a class where mistakes are treated as part of learning.

passage: Last month Rehana had told the class that Delhi was in the south. Half the room laughed, and the teacher had to bang the desk. Since then her hands stayed under the desk during every lesson. Today the teacher asked about the rivers of the north. Rehana knew the answer, because she had read it three times, but her lips only moved. Raghav, who had laughed loudest that day, shouted a guess and was wrong. This time nobody laughed. He looked around, and Rehana saw him swallow. The teacher waited, looking gently in her direction, then moved on to the next question. Rehana's hands stayed under the desk.

qa.q: What had Rehana said about Delhi last month?
qa.a: Rehana had told the class that Delhi was in the south.

qa.q: Why did Rehana keep her hands under the desk even though she knew the answer?
qa.a: Rehana seems to fear being laughed at again, so she protects herself by staying quiet, even though her lips moved with the answer.

qa.q: What could the teacher try to help Rehana speak again?
qa.a: The teacher could speak to Rehana privately, ask for answers in small groups first, and keep stopping mockery quickly so that it feels safe to be wrong.

qa.q: What might Raghav be feeling when he swallows after his wrong guess?
qa.a: Raghav may feel a flicker of the embarrassment Rehana felt, now that he is the one who was wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: A child who was laughed at for a wrong answer stops volunteering, protecting herself by staying quiet while her potential goes unseen.

passage: Marek's turn to read aloud came in three desks. He counted ahead and saw that his paragraph was the one with “muscle” in it. Last term he had said it wrongly and the whole circle had snorted. Now he bent over his desk and searched his bag for a pencil that was already in his hand. Layla, who sat next to him, saw his hands shaking. The teacher said, “Marek?” and Marek shook his head. “Not today,” the teacher said, and moved on. Layla read his paragraph in a rush. At break Marek sat at the far end of the bench, alone, still murmuring the words under his breath.

qa.q: Which word did Marek worry about in his paragraph?
qa.a: Marek worried about the word “muscle.”

qa.q: Why did Marek search his bag for a pencil that was already in his hand?
qa.a: Marek seems to want to avoid reading in case the class laughs again like last term, so he pretends to be busy.

qa.q: What could the teacher try so that Marek reads aloud again?
qa.a: The teacher could let Marek practise the paragraph privately first, and keep any teasing from happening so that reading feels safe.

qa.q: What might Layla have been thinking when Layla saw Marek's hands shaking?
qa.a: Layla may have felt sorry for Marek and wanted to help, which fits reading his paragraph in a rush to take the pressure away.

grounding: A child who was laughed at for a wrong pronunciation stops volunteering and protects himself by staying quiet.

passage:
Monday. Damini watched Ms Varghese hand back the spelling test. “Kabir got six right, up from two,” the teacher said. “That is real work.” Kabir sat up straight.
Wednesday. A boy copied the way Lalremsiami counted on fingers under the desk, and a few children giggled. The teacher put down her chalk. “In this room nobody laughs at how somebody works things out. Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch.” Lalremsiami counted again, openly this time, and got the sum right. The giggling boy went red and looked at his desk.
Friday. Another child got a sum wrong. Damini heard the girl next to her whisper, “Good try, look, you're nearly there.” The teacher, at the board, did not turn around, but she smiled.

qa.q: On which day did the teacher stop the giggling?
qa.a: On Wednesday the teacher stopped the giggling after a boy copied how Lalremsiami counted on fingers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when the teacher said, “Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch”?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt protected but still exposed, since Lalremsiami counted again in front of everyone after being mocked, and the room then watched.

qa.q: What small choice by the teacher on Wednesday did the most to change the room?
qa.a: Stopping the mockery straight away, and then asking Lalremsiami to show the method, so that the child who was laughed at was heard and not shamed further.

qa.q: What might Damini have noticed about how the teacher's habits spread by Friday?
qa.a: Damini noticed that a girl now whispered, “Good try,” to the child beside her after a wrong sum, the same effort-praising tone the teacher used, which shows children copy what the teacher does.

grounding: A teacher who praises effort, stops mockery quickly and applies the same rules to everyone sets a climate that children copy, seen by a pupil.

passage: “Come here, my little Zoya, and I'll tell you about Mr Anand,” said Nani Salma. “When I was ten, our teacher was Mr Anand, and our class had a girl called Meena who read very slowly. One day a boy began copying her, and the room laughed. Mr Anand did not shout. He walked to the back, stood beside Meena's desk and said, 'In this room everyone gets the time they need. Meena, please begin again.' We waited. Meena finished, red in the face, and he said, 'Thank you. Well read.' Next day my bench-mate Hafsa told a shy boy, 'Take your time.' I heard myself say it too. We had copied him without knowing.”

qa.q: Where did Mr Anand stand when he spoke to the class about Meena?
qa.a: Mr Anand stood beside Meena's desk at the back of the room.

qa.q: What might Meena have felt while the class waited for her to finish?
qa.a: Meena probably felt nervous and exposed but also supported, since Meena finished red in the face and was thanked for reading well.

qa.q: What could a teacher do today when a child is mocked for reading slowly?
qa.a: A teacher could stop it calmly, stand near the child, give the child time to read and thank them for it, as Mr Anand did.

qa.q: How might the boy who copied Meena have felt when the teacher spoke?
qa.a: The boy may have felt caught and ashamed, since the room stopped laughing and the teacher's calm words made the copying look unwelcome.

grounding: An elder remembers a teacher who stopped mockery calmly and treated everyone the same, and how the children copied his manner.

passage: On the first Monday of term, the teacher at the village school did not read out rules. She gave each child a slip of paper. “Write one thing that would help us learn together,” she said. Arohi, who had been laughed at before for reading slowly, wrote “No mocking” with a shaking pencil. Mehak wrote “Listen when others talk.” A boy called Sunil wrote “No rules,” and the class giggled. The teacher read them all out, and the children voted on the list with raised hands. Sunil grudgingly raised his. The chart went up beside the blackboard with every child's thumbprint. A week later Mehak told a boy who was talking over Arohi, “That's our rule.”

qa.q: What did Arohi write on her slip of paper?
qa.a: Arohi wrote “No mocking” on her slip.

qa.q: Why did Arohi's pencil shake when she wrote “No mocking”?
qa.a: Arohi had been laughed at before for reading slowly, so writing the rule seems to have taken courage and mattered a lot to her.

qa.q: Why might the rules on the chart be followed more willingly than rules read out by the teacher?
qa.a: The children wrote and voted on them and pressed their thumbprints on the chart, so the rules feel like theirs and not something imposed.

qa.q: What might Sunil be thinking when he grudgingly raises his hand for the list?
qa.a: Sunil may still be unsure about rules but does not want to be the only one left out, so he goes along; being part of the vote may make the chart feel a little his too.

grounding: A teacher and class create shared rules together, such as listening and no mocking, and the children follow them because they helped make them.

passage: In Mrs Greene's classroom, the second Friday of the school year was spent building a class charter. Yosef held the marker. The children shouted ideas: “Listen to each other,” “Raise a hand,” “No making fun.” Ivan called out “No homework on Fridays,” and everybody laughed, including the teacher. “Let's try to keep it about how we treat each other,” she said. Ivan shrugged, then suggested “Say sorry when you mess up,” and the class cheered. Everyone signed the poster. The following week, when Ivan interrupted a quiet girl, Yosef pointed at the poster without a word. Ivan went pink, sat back and said, “Sorry. Go on.”

qa.q: Who held the marker while the class built the charter?
qa.a: Yosef held the marker.

qa.q: Why might Ivan have suggested “Say sorry when you mess up”?
qa.a: Ivan probably wanted to help make a rule the class would really use after the joke about Friday homework was set aside, which shows he took part in the making.

qa.q: What made the poster work when Ivan interrupted a quiet girl?
qa.a: The class had made and signed the poster together, so a silent point from Yosef was enough to remind Ivan of a rule he had helped write.

qa.q: What might the quiet girl have felt when Ivan said, “Sorry. Go on”?
qa.a: The girl probably felt relieved and heard, since the interruption stopped and she was invited to continue. 🙂

grounding: A teacher and class write shared agreements, and children follow rules they helped make more willingly than imposed ones.

passage:
Monday. Vandana gave a perfect imitation of the maths teacher's cough as he turned to the board, and the class roared. Bhupen banged his desk and shouted, “Do it again!” She did.
Wednesday. The test papers came back. Vandana held hers up. “Nineteen out of fifty! I'm a legend!” Twenty voices cheered. Only the girl beside her, who had scored the same, said nothing and looked down.
Friday. The teacher asked her to stay behind. “Your timing is very good,” he said quietly. “I'd like it in the debate club. And come on Thursdays after school. We'll go through the sums together.” Vandana laughed, but her hands gripped her bag.

qa.q: What did Vandana say when she held up her test paper on Wednesday?
qa.a: Vandana said, “Nineteen out of fifty! I'm a legend!”

qa.q: Why might Vandana joke loudly about her score?
qa.a: Vandana seems to hide worry about being seen as weak in studies, and the class's cheering gives her status when the score might have brought shame.

qa.q: What did the teacher do on Friday that avoided humiliating Vandana?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to Vandana privately, praised her timing, offered the debate club and offered help with the sums on Thursdays, without shaming her in front of the class.

qa.q: What might the girl beside Vandana have been feeling when she scored the same and looked down?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and alone with the same mark, without a joke to hide behind while the others cheered.

grounding: A teenager makes jokes to gain laughs and status while covering worry about studies, the class cheers, and the teacher handles it privately without humiliation.

passage: “Come and sit, Rehan,” said Uncle Wasim, tapping the bench. “I'll tell you about Sumit Sir.” When I was fifteen I was the class clown. The back bench chanted my name whenever I did a voice. Really I couldn't follow the algebra and was scared everyone would find out. One day I turned the teacher's chalk-dust cough into a song. The whole class howled. Sumit Sir didn't shout. He said, “Wasim, keep that voice for after the bell. Come to my desk at lunch.” At his desk he said, “You are funny and you are lost. Let's fix the second one.” The back bench was quiet, and later I noticed a few of them were lost too.

qa.q: Who did the back bench chant when Wasim did a voice?
qa.a: The back bench chanted Wasim's name whenever he did a voice.

qa.q: Why was Wasim so keen to make the class laugh?
qa.a: Wasim seems to have been scared that everyone would find out he could not follow the algebra, and the laughter gave him standing in place of marks.

qa.q: What did Sumit Sir do that helped Wasim without embarrassing him?
qa.a: Sumit Sir did not shout in front of the class, asked Wasim to come to his desk at lunch, named both the humour and the difficulty, and offered to work on the difficulty.

qa.q: What might the students on the back bench have felt when Sumit Sir spoke to Wasim?
qa.a: They may have felt caught out, since they had been encouraging Wasim, and later some noticed they were lost too, which suggests the chanting had covered worry for them as well.

grounding: A teenager clowns for laughs and status to hide worry about studies, the class encourages it, and the teacher handles it without humiliation.

passage: The rain had been falling for two hours, and the class was stuck in the corridor waiting for the buses. The seating chart was taped to the wall, sorted by last month's ranks. Front row: the toppers. Back row: the backbenchers. Lalremsiami, at the top of the list, pressed her folder to her chest. Her latest mark was 88, not 95, and she had not told a soul. At the back, Siddharth sat on the floor with his pen still in the bag. “Why bother?” he said to nobody. “I'm the last-row type.” Two boys laughed and agreed. Lalremsiami glanced at Siddharth, then at her mark, and pulled her folder in tighter.

qa.q: Where did the seating chart on the corridor wall place the toppers?
qa.a: The toppers were in the front row of the chart.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami press her folder to her chest?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seems afraid that anyone might find out her mark was 88 and not 95; as a topper she fears any failure.

qa.q: What might help Siddharth start trying again?
qa.a: Siddharth might be helped by someone who treats him as more than a last-row type, such as a teacher who notices one improvement, or classmates who study with him.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Lalremsiami's place at the top of the list?
qa.a: Siddharth may see the topper's life as easy, not knowing that Lalremsiami hides the 88 and pulls her folder tight; the label works both ways.

grounding: Students grouped as toppers and backbenchers begin to live up to the label: one called weak stops trying while one called clever fears any failure.

passage: In the coaching centre, students of Batch A sat at the front near the fan, and Batch C sat by the door. Hafsa was in Batch C, and everybody knew it. Last week she got the top mark on the chemistry chapter, but the teacher read the marks out by batch and hers sounded like an accident. Zainab, from Batch A, turned to her at the water cooler. “You got the highest? I got fourteen wrong on mine, please don't tell.” Hafsa shrugged, folded her paper small and said, “Don't worry, it was an easy chapter.” Back in her seat, she left the next worksheet unopened and watched the door.

qa.q: Where did Batch C sit in the coaching centre?
qa.a: Batch C sat by the door.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa say “it was an easy chapter” after getting the highest mark?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to have accepted the label of Batch C and expects her mark to look like an accident, so she plays it down and folds her paper small.

qa.q: What could the teacher change so that Hafsa keeps trying?
qa.a: The teacher could stop reading marks out by batch, notice Hafsa's top mark as real effort and look at each student's own progress.

qa.q: What might Zainab be afraid of when she says, “please don't tell”?
qa.a: Zainab may fear that a Batch A student with fourteen wrong looks like a failure, showing that a clever label brings its own fear of falling short.

grounding: A student labelled weak stops trying while a student labelled clever fears any failure, in a coaching centre grouped by batch.
